{{< include latex-macros/macros.qmd >}}

Three key assumptions are required to identify causal effects
from observed data [@hernan2020causal]:

## Consistency {#sec-causal-consistency}

<!-- No slidebreak here: the heading shares its slide with the def-consistency div. -->
:::{#def-consistency}
#### Consistency

The **consistency** assumption states that
the [observed outcome](#def-observed-outcome) for a treated unit equals
that unit's [potential outcome](#def-potential-outcomes) under treatment,
and similarly for control:
$$Y_i \eqdef Y_i(A_i)$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-consistency-well-defined-treatment}
#### Well-defined treatment and violations of consistency

Consistency requires that the treatment is well-defined:
there is only one version of treatment,
or different versions have the same effect on the outcome.
Violations of consistency (e.g., different doses of a drug
being lumped together as "treated")
can introduce [bias](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/estimation.html#def-bias).
:::

## Exchangeability (No Unmeasured Confounding) {#sec-causal-exchangeability}

<!-- No slidebreak here: the heading shares its slide with the def-exchangeability div. -->
:::{#def-exchangeability}
#### Exchangeability

**Exchangeability** (also called *no unmeasured [confounding](#def-confounding-obs)*
or *ignorability*) states that,
conditional on observed covariates $\vec{L}$,
treatment assignment is [independent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/independence.html#def-cind) of [potential outcomes](#def-potential-outcomes):
$$A \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1)) \mid \vec{L}$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-exchangeability-interpretation}
#### Interpretation of exchangeability

Intuitively, exchangeability means that among individuals with the same
covariate values,
treatment was assigned as if at random —
there are no unmeasured common causes of treatment and outcome.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-unconditional-exchangeability}
#### Unconditional exchangeability

**Unconditional exchangeability** ($A \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1))$)
holds in perfectly [randomized trials](#sec-causal-rct).
Exchangeability conditional on $\vec{L}$ (@def-exchangeability) requires adjusting for $\vec{L}$.
:::

## Positivity {#sec-causal-positivity}

<!-- No slidebreak here: the heading shares its slide with the def-positivity div. -->
:::{#def-positivity}
#### Positivity

The **positivity** assumption states that
every individual has a positive probability of receiving
each treatment level,
at every covariate value $\vec{l}$ in the [support](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/notation.html#def-support) of $\vec{L}$:
$$0 < \Pf{A = 1 \mid \vec{L} = \vec{l}} < 1
\quad \text{for all } \vec{l} \text{ in the support of } \vec{L}$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-positivity-consequences}
#### Why positivity is needed

Without positivity,
some subgroups have no treated (or untreated) members,
making it impossible to estimate the [counterfactual outcome](#def-potential-outcomes)
for those subgroups.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-positivity-violation}
#### Positivity violation

A failure of positivity is sometimes called a **positivity violation** or
**practical positivity violation**
when near-zero probabilities occur in small strata.
:::

::: notes

These three assumptions —
consistency, exchangeability, and positivity —
are collectively sufficient to identify causal effects
from observed data.
They are sometimes summarized as
"no interference, no unmeasured confounders, no positivity violations."

These assumptions are **untestable** from the data alone;
they must be justified using subject-matter knowledge.

:::
